paragraphs.heading: What a feedback is
paragraphs.text: A climate change feedback is a natural process that affects how much global temperatures rise for a given amount of greenhouse gas emissions. When a feedback amplifies an initial change it is called positive, and when it reduces the change it is called negative. In the setting of global warming, that means positive feedbacks add to the warming and negative feedbacks diminish it. The names are not a judgment: calling a feedback positive or negative does not mean it is good or bad.

paragraphs.heading: What sets a feedback off
paragraphs.text: A feedback is triggered by an initial change. That change may be forced from outside, or it may come from the climate system's own internal variability. An external forcing is an agent outside the climate system that changes it, and it may push the system towards warming or towards cooling. Some forcings are human-caused, such as greenhouse gas emissions or land use change, and some are natural, such as volcanic eruptions. Emissions are the forcing that causes climate change, and the feedbacks together control how sensitive the climate is to that forcing.

paragraphs.heading: The Planck response
paragraphs.text: The Planck response is the extra thermal radiation that objects give off as they get warmer. As Earth warms, more radiation goes out to space. This is a strong stabilizing response. It is several times larger than any other single feedback, and it is the main reason net feedbacks will stay negative. Accordingly, human-caused climate change alone cannot cause a runaway greenhouse effect.

paragraphs.heading: The sum of the feedbacks
paragraphs.text: Added together, the feedbacks are negative overall, but the sum is becoming less negative as greenhouse gas emissions continue. This means warming is slower than it would be if there were no feedbacks. It also means warming will speed up if emissions carry on at current levels.

paragraphs.heading: Water vapor, snow and ice
paragraphs.text: Physical feedbacks include a less reflective surface, which comes from shrinking snow and ice cover, and more water vapor in the atmosphere. The absolute amount of water vapor rises as the atmosphere warms. Water vapor is a greenhouse gas, so the extra vapor warms the atmosphere further, and a warmer atmosphere can hold still more of it. Feedbacks can also produce local differences, such as polar amplification, which results from feedbacks that include reduced snow and ice cover.

paragraphs.heading: Plants, oceans and carbon
paragraphs.text: Biological feedbacks mostly involve changes in the rate at which plant matter takes up CO₂ as part of the carbon cycle. Each year, plants and the ocean take up more than half of CO₂ emissions through the carbon cycle. Over the long term that percentage will fall, as carbon sinks become saturated and higher temperatures bring effects like drought and wildfires.

paragraphs.heading: What is still uncertain
paragraphs.text: The strengths of feedbacks are estimated with global climate models, and the estimates are calibrated against observations whenever possible. The basic relationships are well understood, but some areas remain uncertain, particularly cloud feedbacks. In the carbon cycle, the uncertainty comes from large rates in both directions: plants absorb CO₂ at a large rate, and it is released at a large rate when biomass burns or decays. Thawing permafrost, for instance, produces both CO₂ and methane in ways that are hard to model. Timing differs too: some feedbacks affect climate sensitivity rapidly, while the ice sheets' feedback response stretches over several centuries.
